evidenceAudit.scope: Children from 2 months to 5 years attending a Saudi primary health centre, well-baby clinic or outpatient department: developmental surveillance at every visit using milestone checklists, standardised screening with the Ages and Stages Questionnaire at 9, 18 and 30 months, earlier screening for preterm and very low birth weight infants, what counts as a concern, and referral for hearing, specialist and early-intervention assessment. Uses the 2022 revised United States CDC milestone checklists, the American Academy of Pediatrics 2020 report and three Saudi studies. Not for children over 5 years, diagnosis of specific disorders such as autism or cerebral palsy, or neonatal neurological assessment.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-20.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health national developmental screening guideline was found; the pathway follows United States documents (CDC 2022 checklists, American Academy of Pediatrics 2020), so the ages and schedule are not Saudi-specific. The Saudi well-baby schedule and the Ministry of Health child health record should be checked before local adoption.

The American Academy of Pediatrics report was read from its abstract only (full text is not open access); the 9-, 18- and 30-month screening schedule and the 4- to 5-year attention are quoted from the abstract and from the Saudi paper that cites it.
The Zubler paper was read from its abstract only; the 75% expectation rule for milestones comes from the abstract. The full list of age-by-age milestones comes from the CDC web pages, not the paper.
CDC checklists were not found for the 12-month page under the 12-months address; the 1-year page was used. The 1-year list matches the 12-month visit.

The Ages and Stages Questionnaire third edition in Arabic is the screening tool assessed in Saudi studies, but its Saudi norms and cut-offs have not been established nationally: a Riyadh study of 48 preterm infants (77.1% at risk) was explicitly a feasibility study and a Riyadh very-low-birth-weight study (61 infants, 42.6% abnormal) used 1 standard deviation cut-offs. Sensitivity of the tool is reported to range from 20% to 75% and specificity 76% to 81%, so screening can miss children.

The only Saudi prevalence figures read are: 17.4% developmental delay in preschool children (cited second hand), 45.5% speech delay in children under 7 (cited second hand) and a Taif study of 400 children where 17.9% needed monitoring and 20.4% further assessment on the communication domain.
Autism-specific screening (for example the Modified Checklist for Autism in Toddlers) and universal hearing and vision screening schedules were not sourced and are only referred to.
Local early-intervention services and referral pathways in Saudi Arabia, and the cut-off ages for referral by milestone, were not found; confirm with the regional developmental paediatric service.
Figures were read by automated extraction of the articles and web pages; spot-check each number against the source during clinical review.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so no medicine registration was checked.

pathophysiology.summary: Developmental delay occurs when a child does not reach expected milestones; language delay is the commonest concern (Taif language delay study, Section Abstract). Developmental disorders include autism, deafness or hard-of-hearing, intellectual and motor disabilities, behavioural conditions and those seen in other medical conditions (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract). Preterm birth raises risk of delay in every domain: 77.1% of 48 Saudi preterm infants screened at 4 months corrected age were at risk in at least one domain, and 42.6% of 61 very low birth weight infants at 18 to 24 months (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Abstract; Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Abstract). Hearing problems, family history of speech delay, male sex, autism and motor impairment are associated with speech delay in Saudi children (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).

symptoms: Parent concern about speech, understanding, movement, play or behaviour (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).
Loss of skills the child once had (CDC milestone checklists, Section Act Early signs).
Not meeting one or more age milestones (CDC milestone checklists, Section Act Early signs).
physicalSigns: Does not make sounds other than crying, or does not react to loud sounds at 2 months (CDC milestone checklists, Section 2 months).
Does not sit without support at 9 months (CDC milestone checklists, Section 9 months).
Does not walk without holding on at 18 months (CDC milestone checklists, Section 18 months).
Does not talk in conversation or ask questions at 3 years (CDC milestone checklists, Section 3 years).
redFlags: Any loss of previously acquired skills: act early and arrange urgent assessment (CDC milestone checklists, Section Act Early signs).

Not meeting one or more milestones: do not wait and see; perform a standardised screen or refer directly (Evidence-informed milestones, Section Abstract; AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).

Preterm or very low birth weight infant: screen earlier, with Arabic ASQ-3 as early as 4 months corrected age, and refer any infant with abnormal brain imaging or perinatal events (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Introduction; Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Abstract).
Hearing impairment or recurrent ear infections with delayed speech: refer for hearing assessment (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).
precipitants: Preterm birth and very low birth weight (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Abstract).
Perinatal events and periventricular leukomalacia (Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Abstract).
Family history of speech delay, autism, hearing or motor impairment (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).
Male sex (Taif language delay study, Section Results).
Limited language exposure, low socioeconomic resources, chronic illness or long hospital stay (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Milestones are set so that at least 75% of children reach them by the visit age; a child who meets them is not delayed (Evidence-informed milestones, Section Abstract).
Slower speech with other domains normal; check hearing and family history (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).
Delay in two or more domains before 5 years (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Introduction).
Delayed communication with reduced social interaction; needs specific screening and specialist assessment (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).
Even mild or intermittent hearing loss delays speech (Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).

ruleIn.testName: Arabic Ages and Stages Questionnaire, third edition (A-ASQ-3)
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Developmental delay in communication, gross motor, fine motor, problem-solving and personal-social domains
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Domain score below 2 standard deviations (high risk) or between 1 and 2 standard deviations (monitoring zone)
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Parent-completed screen; sensitivity near 75% to 100% in some studies but only 20% to 60% in others, so a normal result does not remove concern (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Methods; Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Introduction).
ruleIn.normalValue: All five domain scores above the monitoring cut-off

ruleIn.testName: Cranial ultrasound or brain imaging report review (preterm infants)
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Brain injury as a cause of delay
ruleIn.targetCondition: Periventricular leukomalacia, severe intraventricular haemorrhage, hydrocephalus
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Periventricular leukomalacia or intraventricular haemorrhage grade 3 or 4
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Central nervous system abnormalities and periventricular leukomalacia were independent predictors of delay in Saudi preterm infants (Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Discussion).

clinicalManagement.title: Ask about parental concerns and review risks
actions: Ask the parent about concerns and any lost skills (CDC milestone checklists, Section Act Early signs).
Note prematurity, birth weight, perinatal events and family history (Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Abstract).

clinicalManagement.title: Check milestones for the visit age
actions: Use the CDC checklist for the visit age and observe the child where possible (CDC milestone checklists, Section Age pages).
Treat a missed milestone as a reason to act, not to wait (Evidence-informed milestones, Section Abstract).

clinicalManagement.title: Do a standardised screen
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 9, 18 and 30 months, and whenever there is a concern
actions: Use a parent-completed validated questionnaire such as the Arabic Ages and Stages Questionnaire (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract; Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Introduction).

For preterm or very low birth weight infants screen earlier, from 4 months corrected age, and again at 18 to 24 months (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Introduction; Riyadh preterm screening study, Section Abstract).

clinicalManagement.title: Act on an abnormal result or concern
actions: Arrange hearing assessment, and refer to developmental paediatric and early intervention services (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract; Taif language delay study, Section Discussion).
Provide parents with simple play and language activities and follow up the monitoring zone (Taif language delay study, Section Results).
If development regresses, arrange urgent specialist assessment (CDC milestone checklists, Section Act Early signs).

clinicalManagement.title: Review before school entry
actions: Give special attention to surveillance at the 4- to 5-year visit, completing screening if any concern, and share information with nursery or school staff (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is used in developmental screening. Treatment of the cause of delay (for example thyroid, epilepsy or attention disorders) belongs to the specific topic. SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so no medicine registration was checked.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: At every health supervision visit (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).
At 9, 18 and 30 months, and at any visit when surveillance raises a concern (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).
At the 4- to 5-year visit, with screening if there is any concern (AAP surveillance and screening report, Section Abstract).
At least 75% of children achieve each milestone by the visit age (Evidence-informed milestones, Section Abstract).

In the Arabic Ages and Stages Questionnaire, a domain score below 1 standard deviation is the monitoring zone and below 2 standard deviations is high risk for delay (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Methods).
Delay in two or more domains before 5 years (Arabic ASQ-3 preterm study, Section Introduction).

values: Makes sounds other than crying; reacts to loud sounds

Takes turns making sounds; blows raspberries; squeals
Rolls tummy to back; leans on hands when sitting
Makes sounds like mamama and bababa; lifts arms to be picked up
Sits without support; gets to a sitting position by herself
Waves bye-bye; calls a parent mama or dada; understands no
Pulls up to stand; walks holding furniture
Tries three or more words besides mama and dada; follows one-step directions without gestures
Walks without holding on; scribbles; climbs on and off a couch
Says at least two words together; points to two body parts
Kicks a ball; runs; walks up a few stairs
Two back-and-forth exchanges; asks who, what, where, why; speech understood most of the time
Strings items together; puts on some clothes; uses a fork
Tells a story with two events; keeps a conversation going; uses rhymes
Hops on one foot; buttons some buttons

learningObjectives: Perform surveillance at every visit and standardised screening at 9, 18 and 30 months.
Act on a missed milestone or lost skill without waiting.
Refer for hearing and developmental assessment.
pitfalls: Wait and see after a missed milestone.
Relying on a single normal screen.
keyPoints: Milestones are what most children (75%) achieve by the visit age.
A normal screen does not exclude delay.
Preterm infants carry the highest risk.

Tell us at once if your child loses a skill.

Read books with the child daily.
